1.pericope_label: Son of man, write thee the name of the day, even of this same day: the king of Babylon set himself against Jerusalem this same day
debates: How the news reached the prophet
Why the date was to be written down
outliers: Gill and Wesley reckon the year from the captivity of Jehoiachin, which coincided with the reign of Zedekiah, so that it may be named either way
Ellicott rejects outright the supposition that tidings reached the prophet in the ordinary way, since the verse insists he knew on the day it happened
Henry takes the memorandum as a means of confirming the commission of the prophet, since one right in his news may be inferred right in his predictions
Keil and Delitzsch say the exiles and the besieged alike were to learn from the time and the result that the destruction was not to be ascribed to chance
themes: A day afterwards kept as a fast
Days named only by their numbers
A campaign expected against one city and opened against another
Private sorrow said to be absorbed in public calamity

3.pericope_label: Woe to the bloody city, to the pot whose scum is therein, and whose scum is not gone out of it! bring it out piece by piece; let no lot fall upon it
debates: Whether the parable was acted or only spoken
What the bones under the cauldron are
What the word rendered scum means
outliers: Ellicott holds the passage was not a symbolical action but a parable spoken, and that the cauldron carries the article because the people had themselves called their city one
Ellicott refuses to force the sense of the bones and translates literally, leaving the ambiguity of the original as to whether they are burned on the fuel or used as it
Wesley takes the bones as those of innocents murdered in the city rather than as refuse of the cauldron
Ellicott reports that the word for scum occurs five times here and nowhere else, and follows the old Greek version in giving rust
themes: A city that had boasted of being a cauldron taken at its word
Blood laid on bare rock and left uncovered
Judgments that were partial before and complete now
A purification of metal vessels read as the destruction of a city

15.pericope_label: Son of man, behold, I take away from thee the desire of thine eyes with a stroke: yet neither shalt thou mourn nor weep, neither shall thy tears run down
debates: Whether the tire of the head is priestly or ordinary dress
Why a priest allowed to mourn his nearest is forbidden here
Whether the tearless grief is a sign or a description
outliers: Ellicott doubts the priestly dress was used in captivity, since the peculiar garments were worn only on duty, and stresses that priests were expressly allowed to mourn their nearest, so that the prophet is made an exception
Clarke reads the prohibition as describing a grief too deep for tears rather than only as a sign
Ellicott reconstructs the sequence of a single day, the parable in the morning, the warning after it, the death at evening and the questions the next morning
Clarke takes the wife as a type of the city, her death representing its destruction
themes: Light cares said to speak while heavy ones are silent
Bread sent by neighbours to a house of mourning
A married state defended as agreeing with the prophetic office
A companion who shared griefs called a happiness in captivity

19.pericope_label: In that day shall thy mouth be opened to him which is escaped, and thou shalt speak, and be no more dumb: and thou shalt be a sign unto them
debates: Whether the people asked seriously or in derision
How long the silence of the prophet lasted
outliers: Gill allows both a serious question and a mocking one, since the people had reason to think the conduct of the prophet was not want of affection
Ellicott makes the silence almost two years, from the investment of the city to the news of its fall; Wesley counts eighteen months
Ellicott holds the profaning lies not merely in the destruction but in the manner of it, the Gentiles entering the most sacred precincts and carrying off the vessels
Ellicott marks a structural break here, the following collection being arranged by nation rather than chronologically, with a markedly more consolatory tone after the fall
themes: A prophet who was himself the sign as well as its speaker
The same preposition traced through two threatenings
A last hope resting on the safety of a building
Travelling dress worn instead of mourning
